faqPage.ctaText: Contact us directly for a specialized answer to your specific case.

items.q: How can I contact Ahmad Aljarrah?
items.a: You can reach us directly via WhatsApp or phone at +962 79 210 1164, or send a message through the contact form on this website. We respond as quickly as possible.
We serve all Jordanian governorates, with our main office in Irbid and case follow-up in Amman, Zarqa, and all Sharia courts in the Kingdom.

items.q: How long does a divorce case usually take?
items.a: Divorce cases typically take between 3-8 months depending on the case type, complexity, and cooperation of the parties involved.

items.q: Can I send my documents electronically?
items.a: Yes, you can send documents with complete confidentiality via WhatsApp or email without needing to visit the office.

items.q: What are a divorced wife's financial rights?
items.a: They include: deferred dowry, Iddah alimony, compensation for arbitrary divorce (if applicable), child alimony (if any), custody fees, and housing fees.

items.q: Do you handle complex inheritance cases?
items.a: Yes, we specialize in complex inheritance cases including estate correction, heir disputes, and proving ownership within the estate.

items.q: What is the difference between Khul' and divorce?
items.a: Khul' is requested by the wife in exchange for waiving her deferred dowry, while divorce is initiated by the husband and the wife retains all her financial rights.

items.q: Does the mother always get custody?
items.a: Under Jordanian law, the mother has priority for custody until the child is 15 years old, after which the child chooses, always considering the child's best interests.
Alimony is determined based on: the father's income, number of children, their ages, and the previous standard of living, with the possibility of later adjustment.

items.q: Do you offer reconciliation and mediation services?
items.a: Yes, we believe in the importance of amicable solutions and provide reconciliation and mediation sessions to resolve family disputes before resorting to courts.
